71: Adaptable and ambitious, humans tend to value power, wealth and fame, and to champion causes rather than defend territory or kin. Humans have no racial adjustments to ability scores, and get a significant advantage when earning experience as multiclassed characters.
72: Short and broad, dwarves tend to be hard-working, remarkably tough, and skilled in warfare. They are at home in underground places, and artful with stone, gems and other earthborn treasures. Gruff by nature, dwarves gain +2 to Constitution but suffer -2 to Charisma. They are also naturally resistant to poison and magic. Fighter dwarves gain an advantage when multiclassing.
73: Elves are graceful and dexterous, inclined toward natural beauty and magical arts. Their long lives (700 years) and ancient culture gives them a long view toward events and relationships. Elves gain +2 to Dexterity but suffer -2 to Constitution. Sharp-eyed, they have bonuses for detecting secret doors and portals. Elves are naturally immune to sleep spells. Sorcerer elves gain an advantage when multiclassing.
74: Born of the wilds, half-orcs tend to favor primitive pleasures and the chaos of combat. They usually have little patience and less book-learning, but excel in tests of strength, instinct and cunning. Half-orcs gain +2 to Strength but suffer -2 to Intelligence and Charisma; Barbarian half-orcs gain an advantage when multiclassing.
75: Halflings are small in stature but great in resourcefulness, dexterity and wit. Unlike their stay-at-home kin, adventuring halflings tend to be curious, daring - and eager to earn gold to spend on creature comforts. Halflings gain +2 to Dexterity but suffer -2 to Strength; their small size gains them bonuses in attacks and armor, but reduces their weapon choices and carrying capacity. Rogue halflings gain an advantage when multiclassing.
76: A Fighter is a professional warrior, able to use all the standard tools of his trade. As Fighters grow in experience, they master special weapon skills or combat moves. Fighters depend on Strength to deal damage and Constitution to take it; Dexterity also helps, especially with certain weapon/armor combinations. Fighter hit die: d10.
77: Barbarians are warriors who rely upon rage and ferocity, rather than skill, to carry the day. When enraged, Barbarians become much stronger and tougher - although only for a limited time. Barbarians can use any weapon, and move more quickly than others; they cannot be lawful in alignment. Strength and Constitution are important to a Barbarian, and so are Dexterity and Wisdom. Barbarian hit die: d12.
78: Rangers are graceful warriors who are most at home in the wilds of nature. Rangers are able to use any weapon, and are skilled at finding enemies and avoiding detection. Experienced rangers can call upon nature's power to cast divine spells. Rangers depend on Dexterity, and on a Wisdom score of 14 or more (11 minimum) to access divine spells. Ranger hit die: d10.
79: Sorcerers are masters of arcane magic, and as they gain experience are capable of great acts of creation or destruction. Sorcerers cast spells through innate power rather than schooling. They may wield simple weapons and may even don armor if they wish to, although constricting body movement makes spellcasting difficult. Charisma determines the number and power of their spells, and Dexterity and Constitution are useful attributes for any lightly armored character. Sorcerer hit die: d4.
80: Clerics channel divine energy to further the will of their god. This energy is often used to heal oneself and one's companions, but it can also be used to harm enemies. Clerics wear armor and can wield simple weapons. Wisdom determines the number and power of a cleric's spells, and Charisma enhances the power to turn undead. Cleric hit die: d8.
81: A rogue can be a brazen thief, a glib trickster, a stealthy spy, or a fearsome assassin - or any combination of these, using the rogue's array of skills. Versatile and adaptable, rogues are especially valued for their unique ability to detect and disarm traps. Rogues wear light armor with no penalty and use suitably stealthy weapons. They depend on Dexterity, plus Intelligence and Wisdom, for many skills. Rogue hit die: d6.
82:
A chaotic evil character is a destroyer. He is often hot-tempered, vicious, arbitrarily violent, and unpredictable, doing whatever greed, hatred, or lust for destruction drive him to do. A sorcerer pursuing mad schemes of vengeance or havoc is chaotic evil.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
83:
A neutral evil character is selfishness incarnate. She does whatever she can get away with, thinking only of the benefit to herself. The rogue who walks her companions into a fatal trap, then loots their corpses, is neutral evil.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
84:
A lawful evil character operates ruthlessly within a lawful-seeming code of conduct. She plays by the rules, but with no mercy or compassion. The cleric who willfully orders an underling to certain death is lawful evil.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or barbarian.
85:
A chaotic neutral character is an individualist, following her whims. She values her own liberty above all. A ranger who enjoys freedom both from society's restrictions and from a do-gooder's zeal is chaotic neutral.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
86:
A true neutral character does what seems to be a good idea. She doesn't feel strongly one way or the other when it comes to good vs. evil or law vs. chaos, except that they all are undesirable as extremes. A barbarian who acts naturally, without prejudice or compulsion, is true neutral.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
87:
A lawful neutral character acts as law, tradition, or a personal code directs. Order and organization are paramount to him. A fighter who is reliable and honorable, but is no zealot, is lawful neutral.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or barbarian.
88:
A chaotic good character acts as his conscience directs him, caring for others but with little regard for laws and regulations or what others might expect. He's kind and benevolent, but he makes his own way. A rogue with a good heart and a free spirit is chaotic good.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
89:
A neutral good character does the best that a good person can do. She is devoted to helping others, but not beholden to any system of law. A cleric who does what is good, without bias for or against order, is neutral good.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a paladin or monk.
90:
A lawful good character acts strictly and unhesitatingly as a good person is expected to act. He combines a commitment to oppose evil with relentless discipline. A paladin who fights evil without mercy and protects the innocent without hesitation is lawful good.
Note: a character of this alignment can't multiclass later as a barbarian.

356: Children of elves and humans, half-elves tend to inherit both ambitious energy and artistic grace - a combination that often makes them rebellious and unpredictable. 357: Paladins are unrelenting warriors for good. As such, they can channel divine power - to protect themselves, to aid others, and to find the evil they are duty-bound to smite. Paladins require Wisdom of at least 14 for their most powerful spells, and depend on Charisma for their spell's power. Paladins must be lawful good. Paladin hit die: d10.
358: Lives of cloistered training and contemplation give monks extraordinary powers - a monk can sense and avoid blows even before they are launched, and dispatch deadly opponents even when unarmed and unarmored. Monks depend on Wisdom for their special offensive and defensive skills, and look to Dexterity to increase their Armor Class. Monks must be lawful. Monk hit die: d8.

431: Strength measures your character's muscle and physical power. High strength enables bonuses for hitting opponents in melee, as well as dealing extra damage with melee weapons. Stronger characters can also carry more. Strength is especially important for fighters, barbarians, rangers, and paladins.
432: Dexterity measures your character's hand-eye coordination, reflexes, quickness, and balance. High dexterity increases a character's initiative, gives bonuses when shooting, and makes it more difficult to be hit in combat. Dexterity is vital for rogues, and is useful for lightly armored classes such as monks, barbarians and sorcerers.
433: Constitution measures your character's health and stamina. High constitution increases your character's ability to take damage, as well as increasing resistance to toxins and paralyzation. Constitution is especially useful to fighters, barbarians, rangers, and paladins; spellcasters also rely on it to maintain their concentration when casting spells in combat.
434: Intelligence measures how well your character learns and reasons. A character with high intelligence learns more skills as she advances in levels. Due to this, Intelligence is useful for any character class.
435: Wisdom determines a character's willpower, common sense, perception, and intuition. High wisdom indicates a oneness with one's surroundings; it also makes a character more resistant to dominating or charming spells. Above-average Wisdom is especially important for clerics, monks, paladins, and rangers.  Divine spells can only be cast by a character with a Wisdom of 10 + the spell level.
436: Charisma measures your character's force of personality, persuasiveness, leadership, and attractiveness. High charisma indicates a character with a commanding presence and strong personal magnetism. Charisma is especially useful to sorcerers and paladins, but clerics also depend on Charisma when turning undead.  A Sorcerer's arcane spells can only be cast by a character with a Charisma of 10 + the spell level.
